viking1.summary: Viking 1 was the first NASA spacecraft to land safely on Mars, touching down on the plain of Chryse Planitia on 20 July 1976. For more than six years it took pictures, reported the weather and tested the soil for signs of life. It still stands where it landed, silent since November 1982.

fate.label: A bad command cut contact
fate.summary: In November 1982 engineers sent new software to help its ageing batteries, but the update accidentally overwrote the data the lander used to point its antenna at Earth. The team tried for months to reconnect but never heard from Viking 1 again.

photo.caption: A Viking lander test model, built like the real thing, on display at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum.

orbit.caption: Viking 1 seen from orbit by the HiRISE camera on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter in late 2006, 30 years after it landed. The lander is the small bright spot with a dark shadow near the center.

viking2.summary: Viking 2 was Viking 1's twin, and it landed on 3 September 1976 on Utopia Planitia, a rocky plain much farther north. It searched the soil for life, watched the seasons change and photographed white frost on the ground in winter. It worked until 1980 and still sits on that plain today.

fate.label: Its batteries wore out
fate.summary: After 1,281 Mars days of work, Viking 2's batteries failed. The team switched it off on 11 April 1980.

photo.caption: A technician checks the soil-sampling arm of a Viking lander on Earth in 1971, years before the twins flew to Mars.

orbit.caption: Viking 2 seen from orbit by the HiRISE camera on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter in late 2006. The lander is the small bright spot with a dark shadow near the center.

pathfinder.summary: Mars Pathfinder bounced onto Mars inside giant airbags on 4 July 1997, landing in Ares Vallis, an ancient flood channel. It carried Sojourner, the first rover on Mars, and sent home thousands of pictures and daily weather reports. The lander, later named the Carl Sagan Memorial Station, still rests where it landed.

fate.label: Went quiet, cause unknown
fate.summary: Its last data reached Earth on 27 September 1997, almost three times longer than its planned 30-day mission. Engineers kept trying to call it, without success. Nobody knows for sure why it fell silent, but they suspect its worn-out battery could no longer keep its electronics warm through the freezing Martian nights.

photo.caption: The Pathfinder lander seen by Sojourner's front camera in July 1997, with deflated airbags around it, its ramp in the middle and the rock Barnacle Bill to the right.

orbit.caption: Part of a HiRISE image from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (released January 2007). Labels mark the Pathfinder lander (MPF) and, lower down, its backshell and parachute.

sojourner.summary: Sojourner was the first wheeled robot to explore another planet, a six-wheeled rover about the size of a microwave oven. It drove from rock to rock near the Pathfinder lander, studying what they were made of. Planned for a week, it worked for almost three months, and it is still somewhere within about 12 meters of its lander.

fate.label: Its radio link went silent
fate.summary: Sojourner could only talk to Earth through the Pathfinder lander. When the lander stopped transmitting on 27 September 1997, the rover had no way left to call home. Its exact final spot is not known.

photo.caption: Sojourner on Mars in 1997, photographed by the Pathfinder lander next to a group of rocks nicknamed 'The Dice'.

orbit.caption: Part of a HiRISE image released in January 2007, with the Pathfinder lander labeled MPF. Sojourner never went more than about 12 meters from the lander, but it is too small to pick out for certain.

spirit.summary: Spirit was a solar-powered rover that landed in Gusev crater on 4 January 2004. Built to work for 90 Mars days, it explored for more than six years and found signs of ancient hot springs. Today it sits stuck in soft sand at a spot called Troy, next to a plateau named Home Plate.

fate.label: Trapped in soft sand at Troy
fate.summary: In May 2009 Spirit's wheels broke through a crust into soft sand at a spot called Troy, and months of escape attempts failed. In January 2010 NASA turned it into a stationary science station, but it could not tilt its solar panels toward the low winter Sun. Its last signal arrived on 22 March 2010, and NASA ended its efforts to contact it on 25 May 2011.

photo.caption: Spirit's own dusty deck and solar panels, photographed by its panoramic camera in October 2007. Dust like this cut the power it could make from sunlight.

orbit.caption: Spirit as a bright dot just left of the round plateau Home Plate, seen by HiRISE on 13 June 2009, about a month after it got stuck at Troy.

opportunity.summary: Opportunity was Spirit's twin rover, and it landed at Meridiani Planum on 25 January 2004. Planned to last 90 Mars days, it explored for more than 14 years, drove over 45 kilometers and found strong evidence that water once soaked the ground. It now rests in Perseverance Valley, on the rim of Endeavour crater.

fate.label: Dust storm blocked its sunlight
fate.summary: In June 2018 a dust storm covered the whole planet and blocked the sunlight Opportunity's solar panels needed. Its last data arrived on 10 June 2018, showing very low power and a very dark sky. NASA kept calling for eight months, sent its final commands on 12 February 2019 and declared the mission over on 13 February 2019. The famous line 'My battery is low and it's getting dark' was a journalist's paraphrase of that data, not a real message from the rover.

photo.caption: Opportunity's self-portrait from March 2014, after Martian winds had blown much of the dust off its solar panels.

orbit.caption: Opportunity is the tiny blip inside the white square, in Perseverance Valley, seen by HiRISE on 20 September 2018 after the dust storm had cleared.

phoenix.summary: Phoenix was a lander that touched down in the Martian arctic on 25 May 2008. Its robotic arm dug trenches that uncovered water ice just under the soil, and it spotted snow falling from Martian clouds. It went silent as winter arrived and still sits on the icy plain where it landed.

fate.label: Arctic winter took its sunlight
fate.summary: As the arctic autumn arrived, the Sun sank lower and Phoenix's solar panels made less and less power. Its last signal reached Earth on 2 November 2008, and NASA ended the mission on 10 November 2008. Orbiters listened for it again in 2010 but heard nothing, and HiRISE photos suggested that the weight of carbon-dioxide frost had broken its solar panels.

photo.caption: Phoenix's deck in May 2008, with the American flag and a mini-DVD of Mars stories and art. One of its round solar panels is at the left, and the arctic plain stretches beyond.

orbit.caption: HiRISE views of Phoenix from orbit before winter (20 July 2008) and after (7 May 2010). In 2010 the lander is dusty and the shadow of one solar panel is missing, a sign the panel collapsed.

insight.summary: InSight was a lander that touched down on the flat plain of Elysium Planitia on 26 November 2018. Its super-sensitive seismometer recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes, which let scientists map the inside of Mars, from crust to core. It still sits on that plain, its solar panels covered in dust.

fate.label: Dust covered its solar panels
fate.summary: Over four years, dust slowly piled up on InSight's solar panels, and its power dropped lower and lower. It last talked to Earth on 15 December 2022. After it missed two contacts in a row, NASA declared the mission over on 21 December 2022.

photo.caption: InSight's final selfie, taken on 24 April 2022, with its solar panels covered in dust.

orbit.caption: InSight seen from orbit by HiRISE on 11 December 2018, two weeks after landing, along with its heat shield and parachute.

ingenuity.summary: Ingenuity was a small helicopter that rode to Mars under Perseverance's belly and became the first aircraft to make a powered, controlled flight on another planet, on 19 April 2021. It was planned for five test flights but flew 72 times, scouting the way for its rover partner. It now sits with broken rotor blades on a sandy spot nicknamed Valinor Hills.

fate.label: Broke its rotor blades landing
fate.summary: On its 72nd flight, on 18 January 2024, Ingenuity flew over smooth, almost featureless sand. Investigators think its navigation camera could not find enough landmarks to track, so it landed hard and broke its rotor blades. NASA ended the mission on 25 January 2024. Its last contact, relayed through Perseverance, was on 16 April 2024, and it was left set to keep recording data.

photo.caption: Ingenuity standing on Mars on 5 April 2021, two weeks before its first flight, in a close-up taken by Perseverance's Mastcam-Z cameras.

mars-polar-lander.summary: Mars Polar Lander was meant to be the first spacecraft to land near Mars's south pole, to dig into its icy, layered ground. It went quiet as planned while entering the atmosphere on 3 December 1999, and it was never heard from again. Scientists believe it crashed, but its wreck has never been confirmed in orbiter photos.

fate.label: Engines shut off too early
fate.summary: Contact ended as planned just before it entered the atmosphere on 3 December 1999, and no signal ever came back. Investigators concluded that the most likely cause was a software flaw: the jolt of its landing legs unfolding was read as touchdown, so the computer shut off the engines about 40 meters above the ground. It probably hit the surface at about 80 km/h.

photo.caption: An artist's picture of Mars Polar Lander working on the icy ground near the south pole, as it was meant to.

deep-space-2.summary: Deep Space 2 was a pair of small test probes, named Amundsen and Scott, that rode to Mars with Mars Polar Lander. They were built to smash into the ground at about 200 meters per second and check the soil for water ice. They hit somewhere near Mars's south pole on 3 December 1999, but no one ever heard from them.

fate.label: Never heard from after impact
fate.summary: The probes separated from Mars Polar Lander just before arrival on 3 December 1999, and no signal was ever received from either one. Because there was no data at all, investigators could only list possible causes, such as the probes' radios or batteries not surviving the impact.

photo.caption: A Jet Propulsion Laboratory worker checks one of the Deep Space 2 microprobes in Florida in November 1998, before launch.

mars-climate-orbiter.summary: Mars Climate Orbiter was a weather satellite built to study the Martian air and relay messages for Mars Polar Lander. On 23 September 1999, as it fired its engine to go into orbit, it flew much too close to Mars and was lost. It probably burned up in the atmosphere or flew back out into space, so its location is unknown.

fate.label: Mixed-up units sent it off course
fate.summary: A piece of ground software reported thruster data in imperial units (pound-force seconds), but the navigation team's software expected metric units (newton-seconds). The small errors added up over the nine-month trip, so on 23 September 1999 the orbiter passed about 57 km above Mars instead of the planned 140 to 150 km. It was never heard from again.

photo.caption: An artist's picture of Mars Climate Orbiter.

curiosity.summary: Curiosity is a car-sized rover that landed in Gale crater on 6 August 2012, lowered to the ground by a rocket-powered sky crane. It showed that an ancient lake there could have supported microbes. It is still at work, climbing the slopes of Mount Sharp and reading its rock layers like a history book of Mars.

fate.label: Still exploring Mount Sharp
fate.summary: Curiosity is still working, powered by heat from decaying plutonium, so dust storms cannot shut it down. It keeps climbing Mount Sharp, drilling rocks and checking the weather. In 2025 it reached a region of 'boxwork' ridges that scientists think formed when groundwater flowed through cracks in the rock long ago.

photo.caption: Curiosity's low-angle selfie at the 'Buckskin' drill site on lower Mount Sharp, taken with the camera on its arm on 5 August 2015.

orbit.caption: Curiosity is the dark speck near the bottom of this HiRISE view, taken on 28 February 2025 while the rover was driving on Mount Sharp.

perseverance.summary: Perseverance is a rover that landed in Jezero crater, an ancient lake, on 18 February 2021. It searches for signs of past microbial life and seals rock samples in tubes that could one day be brought back to Earth. It is still exploring, now on and beyond the crater's western rim.

fate.label: Still exploring and collecting samples
fate.summary: Perseverance is still working. After crossing Jezero crater's old river delta and climbing its rim, it is exploring ancient rocks beyond the crater's western edge and collecting samples as it goes. In June 2026 it passed a full marathon of driving (42.2 km) on Mars.

photo.caption: Perseverance's selfie over a rock nicknamed 'Rochette' on 10 September 2021; the two drill holes from its first rock samples are in the rock.

orbit.caption: Perseverance (inside the yellow circle) with its tracks behind it, seen by HiRISE on 13 June 2026 in an area west of Jezero crater.

perseverance-backshell.summary: This is the cone-shaped backshell and 21.5-meter parachute that protected and slowed Perseverance on its way down to Mars. They were thrown away during the landing on 18 February 2021, as planned. They now lie in the sand of Jezero crater, and Ingenuity flew over to photograph them in 2022.

fate.label: Cast off during landing, on purpose
fate.summary: About 2 kilometers above the ground, Perseverance dropped out of the backshell so its rocket-powered descent stage could finish the landing. The backshell and parachute were designed to be left behind; they fell to the ground, hitting at about 126 km/h. Ingenuity photographed them from the air on 19 April 2022 to help engineers learn how they performed.

photo.caption: The backshell sitting upright in Jezero crater, with the parachute's lines and the parachute at upper left, photographed by Ingenuity from 8 meters up on 19 April 2022.

orbit.caption: HiRISE view from 19 February 2021, the day after landing, with labels showing the parachute and backshell, the rover, the descent stage and the heat shield.
